opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think it comes down to the nature of the field. In a lot of mature grantmaking areas, global health for example, there's a fairly settled picture of what good work looks like. You have outcome metrics, a body of evidence, and established institutions. A program officer can operate with a lot of autonomy because leadership and the program officer broadly share a model of the world, and disagreements are about execution.

AI safety isn't like that. The field is pre-paradigmatic. There isn't consensus on what the core problems are, which research agendas are promising, or even what counts as progress. So almost every significant grant implicitly takes a stance on deep, contested questions. How hard is alignment? How fast are capabilities moving? Is interpretability going to pay off? Should we prioritize technical work or governance? Each grant is a bet on a worldview.

When leadership isn't closely engaged with those questions, you end up in an awkward position. Either you're making those big worldview bets fairly unilaterally, which doesn't feel right when you're deploying large amounts of money on behalf of an institution, or you're trying to get sign-off from people who don't have enough context to really evaluate the reasoning. Then approvals tend to hinge on surface features, like how legible the project is, how established the people are, or whether it looks reputationally safe, rather than whether it's actually the most important thing to fund.

It's also just lonely and slow. A lot of good grantmaking in a young field comes from argument and iteration. You float a strategy, someone pushes back hard, you refine it. If the people who ultimately own the strategy aren't in those conversations, you lose that feedback loop and the strategy drifts. You can't build conviction collectively, and it's hard to make the bold, concentrated bets the field arguably needs. You default to spreading money around in ways nobody can object to, which isn't the same as doing the most good.

So my takeaway was that in an area this uncertain and fast-moving, close intellectual engagement from leadership isn't a nice-to-have. It's what lets the organization hold a coherent view of the problem and act on it with appropriate confidence.

r001.rationale: The response argues that leadership engagement helps the organization make and share grantmaking judgments, but it does not distinguish permission to pursue Cotra’s understanding-oriented approach from a shared judgment that the approach was worth pursuing.

r002.rationale: The response says close intellectual engagement is necessary and describes the value of deliberation, but it does not state that Cotra realized she wanted to be closely involved in her organization’s central intellectual deliberations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that grantmaking in a field like AI safety is just not the kind of thing you can run on autopilot. It's not like, say, funding bed nets, where there's a well-established evidence base and you can set up a program, define the metrics, and have someone execute against them. In AI safety, the core questions were genuinely unsettled. What even counts as a safety contribution? Is interpretability going to pay off? Should we be funding more evals work or more theoretical stuff? Which labs or researchers are actually on the right track? Those are judgment calls, and they depend on your underlying model of how AI development is going to unfold and where the real risks are.

So when I was making those calls, I really needed people above me who were engaging with the same questions at the object level. Not just signing off on my recommendations, but pushing back, saying "I don't actually buy your story about why this matters" or "have you considered that this line of work is a dead end." That kind of friction is what keeps you honest. Without it, you end up in this position where you're the only person in the organization who has a view, and your view just gets rubber-stamped. That felt bad to me, both because I'm fallible and because it meant the organization's money was being deployed on the basis of one person's intuitions without much of a check.

And there's a more practical side too. A lot of the biggest decisions in this area involve real tradeoffs between, like, speed and caution, or between supporting work inside the frontier labs versus independent efforts. Those aren't purely technical questions, they're also questions about the organization's values and risk tolerance. If leadership isn't deeply engaged, you either end up guessing at what they'd want, or you end up making calls that are really organizational-level calls on your own authority. Neither of those is great. So over time I came to feel that for this to work well, the people at the top needed to be genuinely invested in the intellectual substance of the field, not just delegating it.

r001.rationale: She contrasts leadership merely signing off on her recommendations with engaging the same questions, challenging her reasoning, and sharing responsibility for judgments about the organization’s funding.

r002.rationale: She says she needed leadership to engage with the field’s intellectual questions, but does not communicate that she realized she wanted to be closely involved in the organization’s central intellectual deliberations.

astra-6.text:
I think the core difficulty is that AI safety grantmaking involves a lot of judgment calls where there isn’t a generally accepted framework for deciding what’s good. You’re asking things like: What kinds of AI systems should we be preparing for? What could go wrong with them? And which research today would actually help? Those questions are closely connected to how much money you should spend and what kinds of bets you should take.

If leadership isn’t closely engaged with that reasoning, you can end up with responsibility for a program without a shared understanding of why its strategy makes sense. You can make individual grants, but it’s harder to make big commitments or change direction, because you don’t have that common foundation to work from.

So it wasn’t that I needed leadership to weigh in on every grant. I wanted intellectual partners who could challenge the underlying picture, help improve it, and then really stand behind the decisions that followed from it.

r001.rationale: The response says she wanted shared understanding and intellectual partners, but it does not distinguish permission to pursue her approach from an organizational judgment that the approach was worth pursuing.

r002.rationale: She explicitly says she wanted intellectual partners to challenge and improve the underlying picture, communicating a desire to join the organization’s central intellectual deliberations.

sol-6.1.text:
The hard part is that AI safety grantmaking involves a lot of judgment calls where there isn’t an established playbook. You’re deciding which research agendas are promising, which people you trust to make progress, and how to weigh risks that are very uncertain. Those decisions depend on your underlying picture of AI and what kinds of interventions could help.

If leadership isn’t closely engaged with that picture, you can end up with a lot of responsibility without a shared basis for making the decisions. I could explain a particular grant, but really evaluating it might require working through several deeper disagreements. And I wanted leadership to be able to challenge my thinking and help me catch mistakes, rather than having the program depend so heavily on my judgment. That kind of intellectual partnership is difficult to replace with occasional updates or a formal approval process.

r001.rationale: The response says leadership should share a basis for grant decisions and engage with the underlying picture, but it does not distinguish permission to pursue Cotra’s approach from shared organizational judgment that the approach was worth pursuing.
